summary: This RFC discusses algorithms for synchronizing network clocks from a set of clocks that may not be trustworthy. The interest came from cases where normally reliable clock servers turned out to be wrong. It asks for discussion.

eli5.summary: Several clocks disagree, and you cannot trust any of them completely. This looks at clever ways to figure out the right time.

questions: algorithms for clock synchronization over the internet
subtitle: Statistical methods for finding the correct time when some clocks cannot be trusted.

tldr.problem: Network clocks often disagree, and some clocks are wrong due to hardware failure, software bugs, or operator errors, making it unsafe to trust any single clock.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC presents two statistical algorithms—majority-subset and clustering—based on maximum-likelihood estimation to identify good clocks and estimate the correct time offset.
tldr.outcome: Experiments on real Internet hosts and ARPANET paths demonstrate that these algorithms can converge to within tens of milliseconds even when many clocks are faulty or misleading.

facts.label: Experiments included
facts.value: 163 UDP host clocks, 504 ICMP host clocks

today: RFC 956's algorithms laid the foundation for the Network Time Protocol (NTP, RFC 958), which became the standard for Internet time synchronization. The statistical approach to filtering unreliable clocks remains central to modern timekeeping systems. These algorithms are used by NTP and its successor, NTPv4, which continues to synchronize networks worldwide to within milliseconds or better.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 956 addresses a practical problem in the early Internet: determining accurate time from a network of clocks when some clocks are faulty or unreliable. The motivation arose from real incidents where highly trusted, accurate clock servers turned out to be wrong after power disruptions. Other sources of error include hardware failures, software defects, operator mistakes, and random errors introduced by network delays.

The RFC proposes algorithms based on stochastic models and maximum-likelihood estimation. The idea is that the majority of clocks are reasonably accurate and cluster around the true time, while a minority of faulty clocks scatter randomly. By identifying and discarding the outliers, the algorithm can estimate the correct time.

The author describes experiments using UDP Time Protocol and ICMP Timestamp messages to synchronize clocks across the Internet and ARPANET, demonstrating that accuracies in the order of tens of milliseconds are achievable.
sections.eli5: When your clocks disagree, math can help you find the right time. Assume most clocks are correct and a few are wrong. Find the group that matches best, and use their average time.

sections.title: Majority-Subset Algorithms
sections.content:
The majority-subset algorithm works by examining every possible subset of clocks that contains a majority (more than half). For each subset, the algorithm calculates the mean and variance of the time offsets. The subset with the smallest variance is presumed to contain mostly good clocks, and its mean is returned as the maximum-likelihood estimate of the correct time.

For example, with five clocks, there are ten possible subsets of three clocks (a majority). The algorithm computes the mean and variance for each of the ten subsets and selects the one with the lowest variance. As the number of clocks increases, the number of subsets grows quickly—with 20 clocks, there are nearly 168,000 possible majority subsets—but the algorithm is still practical for reasonable network sizes.

The advantage of this approach is that it can be weighted to give more trust to clocks known to be more reliable. The algorithm also handles multiple samples per clock, accumulating weighted statistics before computing subset means and variances.
sections.eli5: If you have five clocks, try picking three at a time in every possible combination. For each group of three, see how much they agree with each other. The group that agrees best is probably right.

sections.title: Clustering Algorithms
sections.content:
The clustering algorithm takes a different approach, suitable when many samples are available. It iteratively discards the single observation furthest from the mean until only one observation remains. The principle is that as outliers are removed, the remaining observations cluster tighter around the true value.

The RFC presents experimental results using this algorithm on real Internet data. One experiment collected 163 clock readings using UDP Time Protocol (one-second precision). The algorithm rapidly discarded outliers: the first step removed an observation nearly 10 hours off (likely equipment failure), the next two removed observations about one hour off (probable operator mistakes). By the time 50 samples remained, the error had shrunk to about 4 seconds. By 20 samples, the error was about one second with negligible variance.

A second experiment used ICMP Timestamp messages (millisecond precision) on 504 hosts, with much noisier data. Half the clocks were more than one minute off, over 100 were more than one hour off. Despite this, the clustering algorithm converged to within 8 milliseconds of the reference time.
sections.eli5: Start with all the clock readings. Find the one that disagrees the most with the others and throw it away. Do this over and over, and the remaining clocks will all agree.

sections.title: Application to Network Time Synchronization
sections.content:
The RFC describes experiments using both majority-subset and clustering algorithms to synchronize clocks between two WIDEBAND/EISN gateways equipped with WWVB radio clocks (atomic time reference) and connected to the ARPANET. These gateways could measure clock offsets with millisecond precision via ICMP Timestamp messages.

The experiments involved 1000 message exchanges between gateways. Despite occasional measurement errors as large as several seconds (due to ARPANET path delays), both algorithms achieved remarkable accuracy:

  • Raw measurements showed errors of hundreds of milliseconds and variances in the millions.
  • After filtering with a C(5,3) majority-subset algorithm (picking the best group of three out of five), errors shrank to tens of milliseconds with variances under 400.
  • Clustering algorithms showed similar convergence, with final estimates within tens of milliseconds even though raw data varied by thousands of milliseconds.

These results show that the algorithms effectively separate signal (the true time) from noise (network jitter and faulty observations).
sections.eli5: When you measure time between computers over the network, you get some bad measurements because the network is slow and unpredictable. But the algorithms can filter out the bad ones and find the right time anyway.

sections.title: Discussion and Implications
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the majority-subset and clustering algorithms are essentially filtering and smoothing techniques. They work well when sample distributions match assumptions (that good clocks cluster around the true value and bad ones scatter randomly), but they can produce errors if the data departs far from assumptions.

The author emphasizes that robustness in the face of unexpected data is an important design consideration. The detailed experimental results in the appendix provide qualitative evidence of robustness, though additional quantitative analysis using statistical mechanics would strengthen the conclusions.

The RFC calls for an improved time-synchronization protocol combining the best features of ICMP Timestamp messages and UDP Time Protocol. Suggested features include: flexibility to handle multiple simultaneous queries (using UDP rather than ICMP), precise timestamps with both arrival and departure times, extended time format with fractional seconds beyond the 32-bit seconds-since-1900 format, and metadata about expected accuracy, reference clock source, and synchronization drift rate.
sections.eli5: The algorithms work well in real experiments. A better protocol should combine the best parts of existing time protocols and include information about how accurate each clock is.
